chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Sahl ibn Ziyad and Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, all from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Ali ibn Ri'ab from Abu 'Ubaydah from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him)
Regarding a man who married a woman from her guardian, and found a defect in her after he had consummated the marriage with her

He said: 'If the leper, the leperess, the madman, the madwoman, and whatever defect in her is apparent from a long time, then she is returned to her family without divorce, and the husband takes the dowry from her guardian who concealed it. If her guardian did not know of any of that, then he has nothing, and she is returned to her family.'
He said: 'And if the husband obtains something of what she took from him, it is for him, and if he does not obtain anything, then he has nothing.'

He said: 'And she observes from him the waiting period of him the waiting period of the divorced woman if he had consummated the marriage with her, and if he had not consummated it with her, then there is no waiting period for her and no dowry for her.'

key_terms.الْمُفْضَاةُ: The one with a visible defect
key_terms.دَلَّسَ: To conceal or disguise a defect
key_terms.عِدَّةَ الْمُطَلَّقَةِ: The waiting period of a divorced woman

ai.seo_question: What are the rights of a husband and wife when a concealed defect is discovered after marriage consummation?
ai.summary: In this hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (AS), the concept of *tadlis* (concealment of defects) is detailed, specifying that if a wife’s defect—such as leprosy, madness, or obvious physical flaws—was hidden by her guardian who knew of it, the husband may annul the marriage (*khiyar al-ayb*) without a formal divorce and reclaim the dowry from that guardian. This ruling underscores the Shia jurisprudential principle that the guardian bears financial liability for misrepresentation, while the wife’s status depends on whether consummation occurred, determining her waiting period (*iddah*).
